title: CHAPTER EIGHT. On Sacred Scripture's efficacy
english:
CHAPTER EIGHT
On Sacred Scripture's efficacy

So far concerning Sacred Scripture's interpretation: Efficacy is its property by which it is apt by nature to illuminate, move, mortify, vivify, and perfect the man of God who hears or reads decently, by way of an instrument and of a light kindled and elevated by the Holy Spirit — so that he is thoroughly equipped for every good work.

The Apostles magnificently exalt this property of God's word ([[Romans 1:16 >> Bible:Romans 1:16]]; [[Hebrews 4:12 >> Bible:Hebrews 4:12]]; [[2 Corinthians 3:6 >> Bible:2 Corinthians 3:6]]; [[2 Peter 1:19 >> Bible:2 Peter 1:19]]; [[2 Timothy 3:16 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:16]]–[[2 Timothy 3:17 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:17]]) — a property flowing from the Holy Spirit as principal cause, elevating that word as its organ by its own power ([[John 6:63 >> Bible:John 6:63]]; [[1 Peter 1:23 >> Bible:1 Peter 1:23]], where toward the chapter's end it is also called immortal seed). That Spirit kills the impure spirit, conquers evil, removes Antichrist from the midst, renews all things under heaven, frees the creature from sin, vanity, and curse, illuminates our darkness with its light, and fills the earth with the knowledge of God ([[Zechariah 13:2 >> Bible:Zechariah 13:2]]; [[Revelation 12:11 >> Bible:Revelation 12:11]]; [[1 Thessalonians 2:13 >> Bible:1 Thessalonians 2:13]]; [[Isaiah 11:4 >> Bible:Isaiah 11:4]]; [[Joel 2:28 >> Bible:Joel 2:28]]; [[Ezekiel 36:25 >> Bible:Ezekiel 36:25]]; [[Isaiah 32:15 >> Bible:Isaiah 32:15]]; [[Romans 8:21 >> Bible:Romans 8:21]]; [[Revelation 18:1 >> Bible:Revelation 18:1]]; [[Isaiah 11:9 >> Bible:Isaiah 11:9]]).

This efficacy differs from Sacred Scripture's perspicuity, by which it comes about that not only people of sound mind but even evil spirits clearly understand those senses of it needful to know for salvation — without the Holy Spirit's inward illumination — even though they cannot believe or obey them, but rather dissuade faith and obedience. See Whitaker, chapter 1 On Scripture's perspicuity, and Dr. Festus Hommius, Disputation 62 On faith, thesis 5.

title: Question I: Whether Scripture exerts this efficacy only objectively, or also effectively
english: But here Question I must be weighed: Whether Sacred Scripture exerts this efficacy only objectively, or also effectively?

Answer: in both ways. For (1) it teaches objectively, showing which way of salvation is true and which false, and which faith, hope, and love are pleasing to God. For that reason theologians compare it to a guidepost and a Mercury-statue — who have also pointed out the instrument as 'guidepost,' the sailor's needle at sea, a lamp on the road, and Theseus's thread in this world's Circus gardens — not without Scripture's authority ([[Numbers 21:8 >> Bible:Numbers 21:8]]; [[Isaiah 30:21 >> Bible:Isaiah 30:21]]).

(2) Effectively it confers on those who read or hear rightly what it offers in showing — God, Christ, and eternal life — but exalted and drawn into living operation by the Holy Spirit. For that reason it is compared to an axe cutting when raised by the carpenter for cutting, and to the sword of the Spirit ([[Ephesians 6:17 >> Bible:Ephesians 6:17]]).

title: Question II: Whether the bare letter without the Spirit's illumination leads to God — denied; first reason
english: Question II. Does Scripture simply — insofar as it is grasped only as letter, is an outward testimony, and is contained in outward tablets — lead to God, convert, sanctify, and make blessed without the Holy Spirit's illumination? It is denied.

I. Because if the act of conversion, sanctification, and salvation is to be attributed to bare Scripture apart from and beyond the Holy Spirit's cooperation, it follows that even the Devil himself, and those hardened with that second hardening which Calvin, that most eminent theologian, notes at Luke chapter 11 — the hardened and blasphemous, yet thoroughly practiced in the Scriptures — would be converted, sanctified, and saved. But the consequent is absurd. Therefore so is the antecedent. The reason of the consequence is this: because the Devil and the ungodly no less than godly people possess, teach, and dispute from Scripture simply as it stands in the letters, without the Holy Spirit's cooperation ([[Matthew 4:6 >> Bible:Matthew 4:6]]); they abound in dogmatic faith, yet tremble ([[James 2:19 >> Bible:James 2:19]]).

title: Question II continued: reasons II–III; seven points on salutary understanding
english: II. What converts, sanctifies, and saves us apprehends our soul, draws it, and possesses it. But Scripture on outward tablets without the Holy Spirit's cooperation neither apprehends nor draws nor possesses our soul. Therefore Scripture without the Holy Spirit's cooperation does not convert, sanctify, and save souls.

III. Those who assert the contrary seem to understand little: (1) how salutary understanding comes about; (2) what the requisites are, given which salutary understanding is given, and denied which it is denied; (3) what that intelligible idea is in which the thing to be understood is intimately represented to the intellect; (4) that the thing to be understood and the intellect become one in knowing; (5) that whatever consists in the mind is spiritual and abstracted from every bodily mass and letter; (6) how all these things are at last comprehended in a certain point as in the mind's eye; (7) that faith, hope, love, and that whole chorus of virtues lie hidden implicitly in that spiritual seed — more penetrating than any two-edged sword — as a great oak in an acorn, are preserved, and by a prolific spiritual power, the Lord's Spirit breathing, unfold their branches in the inward and outward man, so that the whole kingdom of God is within us, which is righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit ([[Romans 14:17 >> Bible:Romans 14:17]]).

title: Question III: Whether Scripture can be sufficiently understood for salvation without prior grace-light; duplex lumen
english: Question III. Can Sacred Scripture be sufficiently understood for salvation without prior grace-light? Or thus: Is the Holy Spirit's grace-light prior in the order of causes by nature to the salutary understanding of Scripture?
Answer I. Under the demonstration of the truer opinion I lay, as principle and foundation, the distinction of a twofold light, namely of object and of subject, or instrumental and principal.

Scripture's light as object and instrument is nothing other than its sense, which the native signification of the words suggests to us. For the object to be known is not destitute of its inward light. Just as every object radiates with its own light, or is tinted with color by which it presents itself to the eyes through a species, so also Scripture — as may be gathered from [[Isaiah 8:20 >> Bible:Isaiah 8:20]]; [[Luke 16:29 >> Bible:Luke 16:29]]; [[2 Peter 1:19 >> Bible:2 Peter 1:19]].

(2) Sacred Scripture further shows us another light — namely the subject's and principal light — elevating, applying, disposing, and effecting, both in the human mind and in Scripture, so that its inward light may be known. In natural things this is called the light of reason; in divine things, the spirit of revelation ([[Ephesians 1:17 >> Bible:Ephesians 1:17]]), the light of preventing grace, which Christ himself is with his grace illuminating every person, and is called the light of the nations ([[John 1:9 >> Bible:John 1:9]]; [[Luke 2:32 >> Bible:Luke 2:32]]); on which see 4 Ezra 14:15 and [[Psalm 36:10 >> Bible:Psalm 36:10]] and [[Psalm 43:3 >> Bible:Psalm 43:3]]. See Theodoret and Flacius's Key to Scripture. Compare also [[Psalm 18:29 >> Bible:Psalm 18:29]] and [[Psalm 119:18 >> Bible:Psalm 119:18]], [[Psalm 119:33 >> Bible:Psalm 119:33]], [[Psalm 119:124 >> Bible:Psalm 119:124]], [[Psalm 119:135 >> Bible:Psalm 119:135]].

Since therefore it is plain from the Scriptures that a twofold light is required for their salutary understanding — namely the instrumental as medium, and the principal, which not only illuminates the Scriptures but also illumines the intellect so that it can apprehend that medium, Scripture's light — therefore let spiritual people, who judge all things ([[1 Corinthians 2:15 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 2:15]]), at last judge whether this principal light, as principal efficient cause, does not operate first — not indeed in time, but in the order of nature — so that Scripture's inward light may salutarily exert itself and be poured into the reader's heart unto salvation.

title: Reasons 1–4 affirming prior grace-light: object; seeker; exhibition; opening of seals
english: The reasons for the affirming opinion are these:

1. From the object to be known. For Scripture's sense is that very thing which must be known salutarily. Therefore there must be some cause that manifests it, and so is prior to it in the order of nature. And who will deny that this cause is the Holy Spirit's illumination?

II. From the reason of the seeker and finder. For that without which, as principal cause, Scripture's essence, nature, and form — which is its true sense — cannot be found, precedes by nature the finding of Scripture's sense: since a cause is prior by nature to its effect. But now Scripture's essence, nature, and form cannot be found without the Holy Spirit's gracious light as principal cause ([[John 6:44 >> Bible:John 6:44]]; [[Matthew 16:17 >> Bible:Matthew 16:17]]; [[Psalm 25:4 >> Bible:Psalm 25:4]]). Augustine, Soliloquies book 1 chapter 1: "Everyone," he says, "has sought you rightly whom you have made to seek rightly." Therefore the Holy Spirit's grace-light precedes by nature the finding or knowledge of the essence, nature, and form — that is, of Scripture's sense.

III. From the reason of exhibition and offering. For whoever pours Scripture's essence into the heart so that it may be kept there unto salvation is prior by nature to the knowledge of Scripture's essence: since it is not the chariot that draws the horses, but the horses the chariot; and the sower's hand precedes the sowing itself. But now the Holy Spirit by his grace-light pours into the heart Scripture's essence or sense ([[Matthew 13:11 >> Bible:Matthew 13:11]], [[Matthew 13:23 >> Bible:Matthew 13:23]]; Jeremiah 31; Joel 2; [[2 Timothy 2:7 >> Bible:2 Timothy 2:7]]; [[Zechariah 10:1 >> Bible:Zechariah 10:1]]). Therefore the Holy Spirit by his grace-light precedes the knowledge of Scripture's sense.

IV. From the reason of opening and revealing Scripture's seals. For whatever opens Scripture as a closed and sealed book is, as efficient cause, prior to Scripture opened. For if a barred door is to be unlocked, the key must first be inserted into the lock. But now Sacred Scripture is a closed book to all flesh ([[Isaiah 29:11 >> Bible:Isaiah 29:11]]). Yet Christ and his Spirit with light bear the keys of the house of David suspended from their shoulders, so that he may open and none shut, shut and none open ([[Revelation 3:7 >> Bible:Revelation 3:7]]). Whence Theophylact on John chapter 10: "Because," he says, "in the Holy Spirit the Scriptures are understood and opened, which show us Christ, the Holy Spirit is rightly called the doorkeeper." Compare also Augustine, Tractate 3 on John chapter 1. Therefore the Holy Spirit by his gracious illumination is prior by nature to Scripture opened.

title: Reasons 5–8: instrument; matter of prayers; our inability; first origin
english: V. From the reason of the instrument that moves and directs. For no instrument acts unless first moved by the principal cause and put to use.d Scripture is an instrument, and the Holy Spirit's illumination is the principal cause of Scripture's opened sense ([[Job 32:8 >> Bible:Job 32:8]]; Wisdom of Solomon 7:21 and chapter 8:1; [[2 Corinthians 3:6 >> Bible:2 Corinthians 3:6]]; [[Acts 16:14 >> Bible:Acts 16:14]] and [[Acts 26:18 >> Bible:Acts 26:18]]; [[Deuteronomy 29:4 >> Bible:Deuteronomy 29:4]]; [[Psalm 119:34 >> Bible:Psalm 119:34]]; [[Ephesians 4:23 >> Bible:Ephesians 4:23]]; [[Jeremiah 31:18 >> Bible:Jeremiah 31:18]]). Therefore.

VI. From the matter of prayers. For whatever the sons of God ask in order to obtain from God the salutary, living, and inward sense of Scripture precedes by nature the obtaining of that sense. But now they ask the Holy Spirit's illumination in order to obtain Scripture's sense ([[Psalm 119:18 >> Bible:Psalm 119:18]]; [[Colossians 4:3 >> Bible:Colossians 4:3]]). Compare also the old hymn "Purify the eye of the inward man," &c., and the preface which Luther prefixed to German volume 1 in the year 1539. Therefore we can obtain no living sense of Scripture without the Holy Spirit's prior illumination.

VII. From the reason of our inability. For if by nature a person with no powers can inwardly affirm and effectually will God's word, which proposes its sense to him — which properly, according to Scripture's phrase, is to understand it rightly — then altogether the Holy Spirit's illumination must precede this effectual and inward affirmation in the order of nature, even though they are simultaneous in time. But the former is true ([[John 15:5 >> Bible:John 15:5]]: "You can do nothing without me"; and [[1 Corinthians 12:3 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 12:3]]: "No one can call Jesus Lord without the Holy Spirit"; add [[Philippians 2:13 >> Bible:Philippians 2:13]]; [[Acts 16:14 >> Bible:Acts 16:14]]). Therefore so is the latter.

VIII. From the reason of first origin. For whence Scripture's sense has its principle, thence it is also known. For what is the cause of a cause is also the cause of what is caused. Whence Bernard in a sermon to the brothers on the mount: "You will never," he says, "enter Paul's sense unless you have drunk in Paul's spirit." And not a few of the ancients otherwise: "No one can find God unless he has first been found by God." So Didymus On the Holy Spirit: "No one," he says, "ever receives spiritual blessings unless the Holy Spirit has gone before." But Scripture's sense has its principle from the Holy Spirit's illumination ([[2 Peter 1:20 >> Bible:2 Peter 1:20]]–[[2 Peter 1:21 >> Bible:2 Peter 1:21]]; [[2 Timothy 3:16 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:16]]–[[2 Timothy 3:17 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:17]]). Therefore, &c.

title: Reasons 9–10: against Photinian error; pious antiquity against the Pelagians
english: IX. From false teaching. For a doctrine that is properly the Photinians' error ought not to be tolerated in God's church. But that Scripture can be understood salutarily without the Holy Spirit's prior illumination is the Photinians' error. For Christoph Ostorodt in his German Institution chapter 1 §3 says: "We judge that all those err most gravely and dangerously who think Sacred Scripture can in no way work faith and obedience without prior inward illumination and a singular revelation of the Holy Spirit." But since this Photinian doctrine is false, its contradictory — which we here defend — is certainly true. It remains, therefore, that although Sacred Scripture scatters and communicates a grammatical light and historical light without the Holy Spirit's singular illumination — which even demons and the ungodly can see — yet no one can conceive in his mind an inward and living knowledge in Scripture unless the illuminating, influencing, disposing, cooperating, elevating light of grace, as principal cause, goes before, accompanies, and follows.

X. From the testimony and consent of pious antiquity against the Pelagians, who acknowledged no other light converting a person than the grammatical or historical, and so by moral persuasion only. Against them see Augustine, On faith to Peter, chapter 32: "Hold most firmly," he says, "and doubt in no way, that a person whom neither ignorance of letters nor any weakness or adversity hinders can indeed read the words of the sound law and Gospel, or hear them from some preacher's mouth: but that what he hears with the body he also perceives with the heart, and wills to do God's commandments — no one can, unless God has gone before him with his grace, a good will and power having been given from heaven." So Prosper of Aquitaine, Against the ungrateful: "Let the Apostle," he says, "run through the world, preach, exhort, plant, water, rebuke, insist, enter whatever way he finds closed by the word: yet that the hearer is advanced by these labors is effected not by the teacher, not by the disciple, but by grace alone — grace that does not merely counsel by kindly advice and exhortation, but also changes minds, reforms inwardly, and by creating power fashions a new vessel from a broken one."

title: Reason 11: nature's analogy; Orange II; Ambrose/Prosper; Luther; vineyard; ask, seek, knock
english: So the Second Council of Orange, chapter 6: "If anyone," it says, "says that mercy is conferred on those who believe, will, desire, and strive without God's grace, and does not confess that it is brought about in us from heaven that we believe and will, by the infusion and inspiration of the Holy Spirit — let him be anathema." So either Ambrose or Prosper of Aquitaine, On the calling of the Gentiles book 2 chapter 9: "Let one come to God with God as guide," he says: "it is necessary that we are not even fit to think what is spiritual except through God's grace." So also Luther on John chapter 16: "The matter," he says, "is not handled that way, nor are there so many who have the Holy Spirit and understanding as many invent for themselves — as is clear from this, that although Scripture is had and heard, still the Holy Spirit's revelation is required, which applies light to such reading and hearing, which the intellect follows: though it is true that the Holy Spirit does not effect this without preaching and instruction." See the same in German volume 4 p. 140 and volume 8 folio 134.

XI. From nature's testimony, which by a certain analogy is offered for our opinion. For (1) if wheat is to spring up in a field, first of all a field is required as patient subject, then a farmer who sows, third God's blessing, which puts vigor into the seed and sends it into the field, removes husks, purifies the seed's little body, and raises the seminal power so that it sprouts in another species and multiple fruit. The same is the ratio of the spiritual field. (2) The same is shown by vineyard culture, where first a suitable place is required, second a vinedresser who plants and tends the vines, third God's blessing, by whose power, as of the eternal Word, the vine once created is still preserved and made fruitful. So, that Sacred Scripture may be known inwardly and effectually and practically, first a human soul endowed with intellect and will is required; second the proposing of Sacred Scripture or the outward word as seed; third, that this living seed may be received effectually and vividly by the human soul unto its salutary change as to the intellect's ignorance and the will's perversion — which properly is to understand Scripture rightly — the Holy Spirit's illumination is needed, which as principal cause precedes, accompanies, and follows Scripture itself in the order of nature.

Hence Gregory the Great: "Unless," he says, "the Spirit is present to the hearer's heart, the teacher's speech is idle: unless there is one within who teaches, the teacher's tongue labors outwardly in vain." For this reason those about to read the Scriptures for their salvation should not neglect the Lord's precept ([[Matthew 7:7 >> Bible:Matthew 7:7]]): "Ask, and it will be given you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you."

title: Inferences from what has been said: Scripture reading most useful for clergy and laity alike
english: II. From what has been said we infer:

1. That the reading of Sacred Scripture is by far most useful unto salvation and the discerning of spirits not only for ecclesiastics but also for those in civil life, and so even for those whom the papacy designates as laity — Claude d'Espence acknowledging this in his commentary chapters 1 and 2: "Chrysostom," he says, "rightly exhorts all to the reading of the Scriptures: God willed that even the most unlearned craftsman of all should gain some usefulness." That study is approved from heaven ([[Psalm 1:2 >> Bible:Psalm 1:2]]; [[Psalm 119:2 >> Bible:Psalm 119:2]]; [[Acts 17:11 >> Bible:Acts 17:11]]); and therefore the prophets and Apostles recommended their books not to teachers alone but to the whole church ([[Deuteronomy 17:18 >> Bible:Deuteronomy 17:18]]; [[Romans 1:7 >> Bible:Romans 1:7]]; 1 Corinthians 1; [[1 Peter 1:1 >> Bible:1 Peter 1:1]]; [[1 John 2:12 >> Bible:1 John 2:12]]–[[1 John 2:13 >> Bible:1 John 2:13]]). Whence again d'Espence on 2 Timothy 3: "Let Origen," he says, "observe that John writes to four ages: children, youths, young men, fathers."

title: Errors 2–3: forbidding vernacular Scripture; interrupting biblical reading
english: 2. That the pontificals err who hold that translating Sacred Scripture into vernacular languages is useless, dangerous, even pernicious. So Diego Paiva de Andrade, the Portuguese, in Defense of the Tridentine Catholic Faith book 4 folio 241: "Nothing," he says, "can we now hope from the sacred Bibles made common and turned into vernacular languages except the ruin of piety, the destruction of religion, and the ruin of the faith." And folio 243: "Whoever reads Scripture's bare sentences for the most part drinks deadly poison for nectar." Stanisław Hozjusz, On reading the sacred in the vernacular, p. 664: "Now," he says, "we see it has come about by those translations into the vernacular tongue that women for whom it was more fitting at that time to weave wool have already claimed for themselves also the power of teaching; and if anyone wants to bring them back to duty and sanity, he will have more trouble with them than with the men themselves — since men are not even allowed to be Catholics through their wives, and often the husband is forced to believe what the wife wills." Sixtus of Siena agrees, Sacred Library book 6 annotation 142; Jacobus Ledesma, On the divine Scriptures not to be read everywhere in any language, chapter 3.

3. That those err who interrupt biblical reading. Of this interruption in the papacy Johannes Cochlaeus reports in his Commentary on Luther's acts and writings under the year 1521: "Before," he says, "Emser's book came out, Luther's New Testament was multiplied in a marvelous way by the printers, so that even cobblers and women and any unlearned people who had somehow learned German letters most eagerly read that New Testament as the fountain of all truth — whoever were Lutherans — and by often reading it committed it to memory, carrying the codex with them in their bosom. From which within a few months they claimed so much doctrine for themselves that they were not ashamed to dispute about the faith and the Gospel not only with laity of the Catholic party, but even with priests and monks, and even with masters and doctors of sacred theology."

title: Errors 4–5: forbidding Bible reading to the laity; hanging Scriptures as amulets; Cap. 8 close
english: 4. That those err most gravely of all who forbid biblical reading to those they call laity. For this tyranny is exercised in the papacy. For the Jesuit Juan Azor, Moral Institutions volume 1 book 8 chapter 26: "You ask," he says, "whether the books and chapters of the Bible translated into the vulgar tongue are permitted? Answer: at first glance they are forbidden in the fourth rule, namely that Bibles in the vulgar tongue not be permitted to be read everywhere without distinction. Yet in Spain, in the index of prohibited books published there by the General Inquisitor's authority, the sixth rule runs thus: 'Bibles in the vulgar tongue with all their parts are prohibited.' And in the recent index published by order of Pope Clement VIII, the faculty of granting license to read or keep vulgar Bibles or other parts of Sacred Scripture of both New and Old Testament, even when published in the vulgar tongue, has been taken away." Thomas Harding against Jewel, Article 15 section 2 (in John Jewel volume 1 p. 120) holds the same with others; René Benoist of Angers, Biblical Miscellanies book 3 p. 177; Johannes Bunderius in his Compendium of theological matters title 3 article 3; Johannes Molanus of Louvain in his Compendium of practical theology treatise 3 chapter 23 conclusion 2 p. 221.

5. That those err who believe Sacred Scriptures hung from the neck are endowed with various virtues against the world's dangers, diseases, and demons. Alfonso Salmerón does not dare simply to disapprove this custom of the Roman church (Commentary on Gospel history volume 4 part 3 treatise 42), nor Martin Del Rio (Disquisitions on magic book 1 chapter 4 question 4), Juan Maldonado on John 6, Vitus Miletus in Discussion of 600 errors pp. 51–52, or Landulf the Carthusian in Meditations on the life of Christ part 2 chapter 63: "The word CONSUMMATUM," he says, "is reported by the experienced to be of great efficacy in dangers. And it is said to avail specially against an immoderate flow of blood from the nostrils, if with the same blood the same word is written on the patient's forehead." Other examples of pontifical superstition Johannes Weyer noted in On the illusions of demons book 5 chapter 4, and Martin Del Rio in Disquisitions on magic book 3 part 2 question 4 section 9. Refer here also the Enchiridion or Manual in which are found a devout prayer of Pope Leo, likewise some prayers against all the world's dangers, and a prayer of blessed Augustine and Cyprian, published at Venice by Thomas Membruni — from which it will be clearly seen how maliciously the pontifical Roman church abuses Scripture's words unto superstition and magic.
